Alpha-secretase cleavage generating neurotoxic amyloid beta oligomers

explanation: Improper cleavage of APP by secretases yields long β-amyloid fragments that form extracellular plaques, while hyperphosphorylated tau forms intracellular tangles.

stem: MRI of a patient with Alzheimer disease shows cortical atrophy with enlarged lateral ventricles. Which of the following explains the ventricular enlargement, and which cholinergic structure degenerates?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Hydrocephalus ex vacuo; nucleus basalis of Meynert
Obstructive non-communicating hydrocephalus; caudate nucleus
Impaired arachnoid granulation resorption; substantia nigra
Excessive choroid plexus CSF production; locus coeruleus
Recurrent deep parenchymal hemorrhage; red nucleus

explanation: Cortical atrophy causes hydrocephalus ex vacuo. Cholinergic loss follows degeneration of the nucleus basalis of Meynert, which is why cholinesterase inhibitors are used.

stem: A 64-year-old man has REM sleep behavior disorder, visual hallucinations and fluctuating cognition. Which of the following would be found at autopsy?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Intraneuronal neurofibrillary tangles within the entorhinal cortex
Extensive spongiform neuropil vacuolation throughout cerebral cortex
Cytoplasmic alpha-synuclein Lewy bodies in cortex and substantia nigra
Round argentophilic tau-positive Pick bodies in frontotemporal lobes
Multiple cystic cavitary lacunes within the internal capsule

explanation: Lewy body dementia: Lewy bodies of α-synuclein (with neuromelanin) in the cortex and substantia nigra. Memory is spared early.

stem: Which of the following correctly describes frontotemporal lobar degeneration subtypes?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Amnestic syndrome with early selective hippocampal neurodegeneration
Early visual hallucinations paired with spontaneous parkinsonian signs
Startle myoclonus paired with rapid subacute cerebellar ataxia
Magnetic shuffling gait paired with early urge urinary incontinence
Behavioral variant and primary progressive aphasias with tau or TDP-43

explanation: Behavioral variant arises from frontal damage. Primary progressive aphasia arises from Broca area (speech) or Wernicke area (comprehension) involvement. Pathology is tau or TDP-43.

stem: A 63-year-old woman has rapidly progressive confusion, ataxia and myoclonus. Which of the following sets of findings is most likely?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Medial temporal atrophy, diffuse neuritic plaques, and amyloid PET uptake
Cortical ribboning on MRI, periodic sharp waves on EEG, and CSF 14-3-3
Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal enlargement on cranial MRI
Asymmetric frontotemporal lobar atrophy with knife-edge gyral thinning
Multiple punctate subcortical lacunar infarctions on T2-weighted MRI

explanation: CJD: rapid decline, myoclonus and ataxia, with cortical ribboning and basal ganglia and thalamic hyperintensity, periodic sharp waves on EEG and 14-3-3 in CSF.

stem: A 72-year-old man has a magnetic gait, urinary incontinence and cognitive decline, with enlarged ventricles. Which of the following is the best description of the disorder and its treatment?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Alzheimer disease; central acetylcholinesterase inhibitors
Multi-infarct vascular dementia; aggressive antiplatelet therapy
Dementia with Lewy bodies; low-dose typical antipsychotics
Normal pressure hydrocephalus; ventriculoperitoneal shunting
Sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease; compassionate supportive care

explanation: Normal pressure hydrocephalus: gait disorder, dementia and urinary incontinence from impaired CSF resorption by arachnoid granulations. Treat with shunting.

stem: Which of the following best differentiates vascular dementia from Alzheimer disease?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Stepwise cognitive deterioration associated with focal vascular lesions
Insidious progressive short-term episodic memory loss
Isolated bilateral anterior hippocampal volume loss
Extracellular accumulation of fibrillar amyloid plaques
Marked clinical responsiveness to central cholinesterase inhibitors

explanation: Vascular dementia has stepwise progression and focal deficits from multiple infarcts. Memory impairment tends to occur later. AD has insidious memory loss.

stem: According to your course notes, which MMSE score range indicates mild cognitive impairment?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Above 28

explanation: Per your course notes, an MMSE of 26–21 indicates mild cognitive impairment.

stem: A 42-year-old man has chorea, depression and dementia. His father had similar symptoms. Which of the following correctly describes this disease?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Autosomal recessive GAA trinucleotide expansion; frataxin deficiency
X-linked dominant CGG trinucleotide expansion; FMR1 gene silencing
Maternal mitochondrial DNA point mutation; heteroplasmic inheritance
Sporadic infectious proteinaceous prion conversion; conformational change
Autosomal dominant CAG repeat expansion; huntingtin gene on chromosome 4

explanation: Huntington disease: autosomal dominant CAG repeats in huntingtin, caudate and putamen atrophy, dopamine excess relative to acetylcholine, treated with tetrabenazine.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has a strange sensation followed by involuntary contraction of her right arm. She remains fully aware and can answer questions throughout. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Absence seizure
Tonic-clonic seizure
Atonic seizure
Focal aware seizure
Myoclonic seizure

explanation: Focal aware seizure: focal symptoms with preserved awareness.

stem: A 28-year-old man has a warning sensation, then stares, picks at his clothes and smacks his lips, and does not respond. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Focal aware motor seizure with retained consciousness
Focal impaired awareness seizure with automatisms
Generalized typical absence seizure without aura
Generalized atonic seizure with sudden drop attack
Generalized tonic seizure with sustained stiffening

explanation: Focal impaired awareness seizure: aura plus impaired awareness with automatisms.

stem: A 20-year-old woman in class suddenly stiffens for about 20 seconds, then is sleepy and confused. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Myoclonic seizure
Atonic seizure
Tonic seizure
Absence seizure
Focal aware seizure

explanation: Tonic seizure: stiffening of the body, then postictal drowsiness and confusion.

stem: A 35-year-old man at work cries out, falls stiff, and then has rhythmic jerking of all limbs for about 1 minute. He is incontinent and sleepy afterward. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Tonic-clonic seizure
Absence seizure
Myoclonic seizure
Atonic seizure
Syncope

explanation: Tonic-clonic seizure: alternating stiffening and jerking, incontinence and postictal confusion.

stem: A 10-year-old girl has sudden, brief, shock-like jerks of both shoulders and arms for about 4 seconds, with several episodes a day. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Absence seizure
Tonic seizure
Atonic seizure
Focal aware seizure
Myoclonic seizure

explanation: Myoclonic seizure: brief repetitive jerks of the arms or legs.

stem: A 30-year-old woman who was talking suddenly falls to the ground motionless. She does not respond and is confused afterward. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Myoclonic seizure
Tonic-clonic seizure
Absence seizure
Atonic seizure
Focal aware seizure

explanation: Atonic (drop) seizure: sudden loss of tone and falling.

stem: A 6-year-old boy does not respond when called on in class. He stares to the side, blinks several times for about 20 seconds, and then resumes talking. Which of the following is the best description?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Atonic seizure
Absence seizure
Tonic seizure
Myoclonic seizure
Focal impaired awareness seizure

explanation: Absence seizure: blank stare with blinking, no postictal period.

stem: A student asks how focal and generalized seizures differ. Which of the following is correct?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Both seizure types originate simultaneously from bilateral cerebral hemispheres
Focal seizures invariably cause complete immediate loss of consciousness
Focal seizures begin in one hemisphere, whereas generalized involve both hemispheres
Generalized seizures originate from a discrete circumscribed cortical focus
Focal and generalized seizures display identical electroencephalographic patterns

explanation: Focal seizures start in one area of one hemisphere and can secondarily generalize. Generalized seizures start in both hemispheres.

stem: A 30-year-old man is brought in after convulsing for 12 minutes with no return of awareness. Which of the following defines his condition?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Continuous seizure activity >=5 minutes or recurrent seizures without recovery
Any generalized seizure accompanied by urinary or fecal incontinence
A single self-limited convulsive seizure lasting less than 60 seconds
Two separate unprovoked seizures occurring at least one week apart
Any focal seizure preceded by an epigastric or experiential aura

explanation: Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or recurring seizures without regaining consciousness.

stem: A patient has a transient loss of consciousness. Which of the following lists the four components of a seizure that help distinguish it from syncope and narcolepsy?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Experiential aura, throbbing headache, fever, and maculopapular rash
High fever, nuchal rigidity, petechial rash, and holocephalic headache
Severe epigastric pain, projectile vomiting, diarrhea, and fever
Episodic palpitations, facial pallor, diaphoresis, and presyncope
Premonitory symptoms, abrupt consciousness loss, ictal event, postictal state

explanation: The four components are prodrome, loss of consciousness, physical event and postictal state. Their time course helps separate seizure from syncope and narcolepsy.

stem: Which of the following correctly lists the most common causes of seizures in adults and in children?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Adults: congenital malformations; children: ischemic stroke
Adults: genetic channelopathies; children: malignant primary tumors
Adults: bacterial infections only; children: embolic stroke
Adults: cerebrovascular, tumors, trauma; children: infection, trauma, congenital
Adults: metabolic derangements only; children: metabolic derangements only

explanation: Adult seizures are most often from tumors, trauma, infections and stroke. Childhood seizures are from infections, trauma and congenital defects.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has her second episode of loss of consciousness with convulsive movements. Which of the following tests best detects abnormal cortical electrical activity?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Urine toxicology
Electroencephalogram
Serum electrolytes
Head CT
Tilt-table test

explanation: EEG detects abnormal cortical electrical activity.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has a single seizure, and no identifiable cause is found. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Immediate initiation of dual antiseizure drug combination therapy
Urgent surgical evaluation for anterior temporal lobectomy
Identification and treatment of underlying causes without maintenance AEDs
Lifelong driving and occupational prohibition regardless of EEG
Mandatory continuous inpatient video-EEG monitoring for one week

explanation: After a single unprovoked seizure most neurologists do not treat, but any identifiable cause should be treated.

stem: A 24-year-old woman has her second unprovoked seizure. Evaluation is unremarkable. Which of the following is the best recommendation?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Initiate maintenance antiseizure monotherapy
Reassurance and observation without treatment
Tilt-table autonomic testing
Brain fluorodeoxyglucose-PET scan
Repeat outpatient non-contrast head CT

explanation: After a second unprovoked seizure the risk of a third is 80–90%, so treatment is recommended.

stem: A 40-year-old man has a seizure with fever, neck stiffness and altered mental status, and meningitis is confirmed. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Lifelong maintenance antiseizure polytherapy
Resective epilepsy surgical evaluation
Implantation of a vagus nerve stimulator
Initiation of a strict ketogenic dietary regimen
Acute treatment of the underlying systemic etiology

explanation: A seizure from meningitis, alcohol withdrawal, electrolyte disturbance or fever is provoked, so treat the cause.

stem: A 52-year-old man with focal seizures has fever, a sore throat and an absolute neutrophil count of 400/µL after starting a new antiseizure drug. Which of the following drugs, with its mechanism and adverse effects, best fits?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Ethosuximide; T-type calcium channel inhibition; gastrointestinal distress
Lamotrigine; sodium channel inhibition; isolated skin eruption
Valproate; GABA transaminase inhibition; weight loss and alopecia
Carbamazepine; sodium channel inhibition; aplastic anemia and SIADH
Phenytoin; GABAA receptor allosteric potentiation; sedation

explanation: Carbamazepine blocks sodium channels. Adverse effects include agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and birth defects.

stem: A 45-year-old man on long-term antiseizure therapy has gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, peripheral neuropathy and megaloblastic anemia. Which of the following drugs and mechanisms is most likely?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Valproic acid; GABA transaminase inhibition
Phenytoin; voltage-gated sodium channel blockade
Ethosuximide; T-type calcium channel blockade
Lamotrigine; calcium channel blockade
Carbamazepine; GABA enhancement

explanation: Phenytoin blocks sodium channels. Adverse effects: peripheral neuropathy, gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, megaloblastic anemia, DRESS, lupus-like syndrome and birth defects.

stem: Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of valproic acid?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Selective inhibition of low-threshold T-type thalamic calcium channels
Selective fast inactivation of voltage-gated neuronal sodium channels
Inactivation of sodium and T-type calcium channels and enhancement of GABA
Allosteric potentiation of postsynaptic GABAA chloride conductance
Non-competitive antagonism of postsynaptic ionotropic NMDA receptors

explanation: Valproic acid blocks sodium and T-type calcium channels and inhibits GABA degradation.

stem: A woman of childbearing age takes valproic acid. Which of the following sets of adverse effects should she be counseled about?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Hepatotoxicity, acute pancreatitis, and teratogenic neural tube defects
Agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, and syndrome of inappropriate ADH
Gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, and megaloblastic anemia
Isolated morbilliform cutaneous eruption without systemic signs
Irreversible concentric peripheral visual field constriction

explanation: Valproic acid causes hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis and neural tube defects.

stem: A patient starts a sodium channel-blocking antiseizure drug that must be titrated slowly because of the risk of a life-threatening skin reaction. Which of the following is the drug and the reaction?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Phenytoin; hirsutism
Valproic acid; pancreatitis
Carbamazepine; hyponatremia
Ethosuximide; weight gain
Lamotrigine; Stevens-Johnson syndrome

explanation: Lamotrigine blocks sodium channels and requires slow titration to reduce the risk of Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

stem: A 7-year-old child with absence seizures takes ethosuximide. Which of the following correctly states its mechanism and a serious adverse effect?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Voltage-gated sodium channel blockade; agranulocytosis
GABAA receptor chloride current potentiation; sedation
Postsynaptic NMDA glutamate receptor blockade; psychosis
Thalamic T-type calcium channel blockade; Stevens-Johnson syndrome
GABA transaminase enzyme inhibition; fulminant hepatotoxicity

explanation: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons. A serious adverse effect is Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

stem: A survivor of herpes simplex encephalitis has episodes of a burning smell followed by staring and lip smacking. Which of the following is the most likely origin of these seizures?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Calcarine cortex of the occipital lobe
Medial temporal lobe uncus
Precentral gyrus of the frontal lobe
Lateral hemisphere of the cerebellum
Dorsomedial nucleus of the thalamus

explanation: Uncinate seizures arise from the uncus and olfactory cortex of the temporal lobe, a common site of damage after HSV-1 encephalitis.

stem: A 29-year-old man collapses with a generalized seizure after 2 months of headaches and personality change. Biopsy shows fried-egg cells with a chicken-wire capillary pattern. Which of the following best describes the cause of his seizures?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Neuronal channelopathy (voltage-gated potassium channel mutation)
Systemic metabolic disturbance (acute profound hypoglycemia)
Focal intracranial structural lesion (oligodendroglioma)
Benign genetic syndrome (familial febrile convulsions)
Substance withdrawal syndrome (acute sedative cessation)

explanation: The cause is structural (a tumor), the leading adult cause of new seizures, here an oligodendroglioma.

stem: A 6-year-old girl has staring spells that are reproduced by hyperventilation. Which of the following describes the expected findings?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave bursts with no postictal confusion
Unilateral anterior temporal sharp waves with prolonged postictal confusion
Chaotic, high-voltage, disorganized hypsarrhythmia on background
Periodic synchronous triphasic sharp-wave discharges at 1–2 Hz
Continuous generalized polymorphic delta slowing without spikes

explanation: Absence seizures show generalized 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges, are provoked by hyperventilation, and have no postictal state.

options.text: Trans-synaptic synchronization through the dorsal thalamic nuclei
Trans-hemispheric propagation through the anterior commissure
Descending propagation through the intermediate spinal gray column
Subcortical recruitment through the putamen and globus pallidus
Contiguous somatotopic spread along the precentral motor strip

explanation: Jacksonian march follows the motor homunculus along the precentral gyrus.

stem: A man has a witnessed collapse. Which of the following best supports seizure rather than syncope or narcolepsy?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Immediate complete recovery of orientation within 5 to 10 seconds
Isolated brief non-rhythmic myoclonic jerks at sleep onset
Onset triggered predictably by prolonged upright quiet standing
Lateral tongue laceration, incontinence, and postictal confusion
Marked facial pallor, diaphoresis, and cold clammy extremities

explanation: Lateral tongue biting (bloody saliva), incontinence and prolonged postictal confusion support a seizure. Syncope features quick recovery and a prodrome of pallor.

stem: Which of the following best describes the general principles of treating epilepsy?
source: Neuro E3 Practice Exam 2 High-Yield USMLE Step 1 Style (150 Questions)

options.text: Initiate multiple antiseizure drugs simultaneously at maximum target doses
Initiate monotherapy at low dose, titrating to efficacy or tolerability
Mandate surgical resection prior to any pharmacological trials
Rely exclusively on dietary ketosis before initiating medications
Maintain initial monotherapy at subtherapeutic doses regardless of control

explanation: Treatment aims to eliminate seizures with the fewest side effects and the lowest number and dose of drugs. Start with one drug at the lowest dose and titrate, then add a second if needed.
